subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Regret Aversion
description: Learn Regret Aversion in one minute.

hook.text: You keep a losing stock because selling would make the loss real. As long as you hold, regret stays hypothetical.

buildup.text: Regret aversion means avoiding action to dodge the pain of a bad outcome. Inaction feels safer than a wrong choice.

discovery.text: Zeelenberg found people regret actions more than inactions in the short term, but reverse this over a lifetime.

twist.text: Old people regret things they did not do far more than mistakes they made. Inaction feels safe now but stings later.

climax.text: Ask: will I regret not doing this in ten years? Long-term regret comes from inaction, not from trying and failing.

punchline.text: The safest choice now is often the most regretted later.

quiz.question: What do people regret most over a lifetime?

details.summary: Regret aversion is the tendency to avoid actions that might lead to regret, even when the expected outcome of acting is better than not acting. People choose inaction over action because regret from doing something wrong feels worse than regret from missing an opportunity.
details.whyItMatters: Regret aversion creates a systematic bias toward the status quo and inaction. It prevents people from making changes, investments, and career moves that have positive expected value because the anticipated regret of failure feels unbearable.
takeaways: Anticipated regret makes people prefer inaction even when action has better odds
Regret from commission feels worse than regret from omission in the short term
In the long run, people regret things they did not do more than things they did

faq.question: Why does doing something feel riskier than doing nothing?
faq.answer: Actions have clear causal links to outcomes, making regret feel personal and avoidable. Inaction feels like the default, so negative outcomes from inaction feel like fate rather than personal failure. This asymmetry makes action feel psychologically riskier.

faq.question: How can regret aversion be overcome?
faq.answer: Ask what you would regret more in ten years: having tried and failed, or never having tried at all. This long-term reframing reverses the asymmetry because long-term regret is dominated by missed opportunities rather than failed attempts.
